 First Alert Weather: “Cloud Season” is coming. Here’s why it happens 
 Once we get into November, that’s when cloudy season arrives in the area. By Derek Witt Published : Oct. 28, 2026 at 5:56 PM EDT | Updated : 1 hour ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google TOLEDO, Ohio (WTVG) - Ever since the middle of October, we’ve been seeing a lot of sunshine, barely a cloud in the sky at times for the last week and a half. Through Halloween, we should still see a fair bit of sunshine, but once we get into November, that’s when cloudy season arrives in the area. 
 Check out the historical chance of sunshine here through mid-October. At least half the time, skies are sunny, mostly sunny or partly sunny, but then on Nov. 1, clouds become more likely in the heart of cloud season. That arrives in mid-December each year. Cloud season does continue through January.
 Once we get to February, usually we’re starting to see a little more sunshine try to peek through between any rounds of rain or snow working through the area. So, cloud season is fast approaching. 
 It’s always a sharp drop-off from October into November, from those very sunny days to the cloudy days. But why does it happen? Why do we even get a cloud season? It all has to do with the Great Lakes and the weather patterns that develop as we get into November. 
 The lake water is still warm from the summertime and cold air from the northwest overruns the Great Lakes. As it does, that warm air can rise, taking the moisture with it.
 Then, as it cools off in the sky, it condenses into clouds and that pattern continues. The winds continue to blow that cold air over the warm water. That persistent wind direction forms the sheets of clouds. They develop across the Great Lakes, Michigan, down into Ohio, and all the way into the Appalachian Mountains. Plus, these clouds will last as long as that northwest wind continues, and the lake water stays warmer than the cold air above.
